Q: What was the architecture for the chat application you built at Mobiquity?
A: I built an Agentic Chat UI integrated with a Python backend. We used RestAPI for agent configuration and WebSockets for the live chat functionality. For testing, I implemented integration tests using Playwright and actually set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) as a mock. This was crucial because it allowed us to run comprehensive tests without burning through our budget on API tokens.

Q: How do you handle routing in complex React applications?
A: Recently at Mobiquity, for a dating platform project, I migrated the web-app routing from React Router v6 to v7. I also designed middleware using Axios Interceptors. This allowed us to steer user stories based on browser properties—essentially creating road-blockers during onboarding if specific conditions weren't met.

Q: What does your dev environment look like? Any specific hardware preferences?
A: I run a MacBook Pro 16 M2 and a Mac Mini M2, both with 16GB RAM. For screens, I have a bit of a hack: I use an ultra-wide monitor as my main, but I keep an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen in portrait mode on the side. It's specifically for reviewing mobile UIs. I prefer Webstorm in dark mode—usually working in a dark room.

Q: Tell me about a legacy migration project you've worked on.
A: At EriksDigital, I migrated a massive monolith built on WebSphere to a hybrid micro-frontend architecture. It involved reverse-engineering old modules that were poorly documented. Despite the system constraints, we managed to improve Google Lighthouse performance scores significantly.

Q: Have you worked with React Native?
A: Yes, at DigitalChefs. I built a complex React Native app for the KLM flight crew, specifically for business class to manage passenger food and drink orders. I also created a component library with custom navigation elements and an ExpressJS system to manage the app data and statistics.

Q: What is your preferred tech stack right now?
A: For high-traffic pages where SEO and speed matter, I definitely prefer NextJS. However, for lightweight web projects, I stick to Vanilla JS with SCSS and Vite. My core toolset these days includes TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Azure for deployment, and I'm using tools like Claude Code and Cursor to speed up workflows.

Q: Did you ever do embedded work?
A: Yeah, at ABiggerCircle. I developed entertainment system modules using BackboneJS, jQuery, and Gulp for devices in a closed network environment—specifically for automotive or maritime settings, like ships out in the ocean. I had to build complex audio control logic to manage captain notifications alongside the entertainment systems.

Q: Can you elaborate on your testing strategy for the chat UI at Hexaware?
A: For the Agentic Chat UI, we needed robust integration tests without incurring high costs. I implemented Playwright for the testing framework. To save budget on API tokens, I set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock server. This allowed us to simulate agent responses and test the WebSocket integration thoroughly before hitting the actual paid APIs.

Q: How did you approach the B2B requirements at A-Dam?
A: For the B2B version of the webshop, we needed a distinct flow for bulk purchases. I developed a custom UI specifically for these clients, including specialized checkout options that differed from the standard B2C interface. The core stack remained NextJS, which allowed us to maintain performance while serving two different customer types.

Q: What was the stack you used for the Oil & Gas software in Ukraine?
A: That was at IT-Transit. It was a bit of an older stack—we used Flex and ActionScript along with JavaScript for the engineering CMS platform. I built software tools for landscape measurements and pipe inspections. I also implemented a REST API to connect client services, generating renovation progress statistics based on accepted industry norms.

Q: What was your involvement in the Backend side of the Platform CMS project?
A: While I focused on the notification control system frontend, I worked closely with the BE team on API specs. We utilized a BFF (Backend for Frontend) strategy. My main goal was to steer the backend work so we could generate reliable, shared TypeScript types, ensuring the contract between the layers remained stable.

Q: What did you do at Luxoft during your early career?
A: I was working on Automotive UI for car entertainment systems. My role was to support senior developers with feature development, but I also took ownership of managing the team’s Git repository and the code review process. It was a great introduction to high-standard engineering workflows.

Q: Why NextJS over a standard Create React App setup?
A: For high-traffic projects like the A-Dam web-shop, NextJS is a no-brainer because of SSR and built-in SEO features. It allowed us to make page loads 5x faster. However, if I'm building something lightweight where performance overhead isn't an issue, I'll stick to Vanilla JS with SCSS and Vite to keep the bundle as small as possible.

Q: Tell me about your LLM experience at Mobiquity.
A: I built a chat UI that integrated with a Python BE using LangChain. For the demo application, I had to represent complex banking client data using custom UI elements like charts, graphs, and tables. I'm very interested in local LLMs and private agents, which I'm currently exploring further in my own time.

Q: What was the tightest deadline you've worked under?
A: At Mobiquity, we had a 3-month window to release a dating platform's entire user onboarding and profile pages. I had to design specific middleware using Axios Interceptors to manage 'onboarding roadblocks' based on browser properties. It was intense, but we hit the deadline.

Q: How do you manage cross-browser testing for mobile UIs?
A: I use my Asus 14-inch Zenscreen in portrait mode as a dedicated secondary display for mobile UI previews. It sits right next to my ultra-wide. For automated testing, I rely on Playwright, which I used at Mobiquity to run integration tests against a local LLM mock to keep everything consistent.

Q: Have you worked with PHP or Laravel?
A: Yes, back at ABiggerCircle. I contributed to a marketing campaign builder platform that used PHP and Laravel on the backend, with VanillaJS on the frontend. I specifically worked on a component wrapper that allowed existing components to work within a Drag & Drop view.

Q: What's your preferred way to handle CSS in modern apps?
A: I'm a big fan of Tailwind CSS for its speed and consistency across a team. I used it heavily at Mobiquity. If I'm working on a more traditional project or something very custom, I'll use SCSS, which is what I go for when I'm using Vanilla JS and Vite.

Q: How did you handle the routing migration for the dating platform?
A: We had to migrate the web-app routing from React Router v6 to v7 under a strict 3-month deadline. It wasn't just a version bump; I designed middleware using Axios Interceptors to steer user stories based on browser properties. This was crucial for handling onboarding roadblocks dynamically during the user registration flow.

Q: What tools are you using to speed up your coding workflow these days?
A: I've integrated AI tools quite heavily. I'm using Claude Code and Cursor. They integrate well with my preferred environment—Webstorm in dark mode. It helps me iterate faster, especially when I'm working on boilerplate or refactoring large chunks of TypeScript.

Q: Tell me about the legacy migration you did at EriksDigital.
A: We migrated a monolithic WebSphere application to a hybrid micro-frontend architecture. It was a heavy lift. I had to reverse-engineer old modules that weren't well documented. The big win was that despite the system constraints, we managed to significantly improve the Google Lighthouse performance scores.

Q: How do you manage mobile-first development on your desktop setup?
A: I have a specific hack for that. I use an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen set up in portrait mode right next to my main ultra-wide monitor. It's dedicated entirely to reviewing mobile UIs while I code. It saves me from constantly resizing browser windows or relying solely on DevTools emulation.

Q: What was the architecture for the notification system at Mobiquity?
A: I built the frontend for the notification control system as part of the Platform CMS. I configured the Azure deployment pipelines for it myself. A big part of that work was collaborating with the Backend team to define the API specs using a BFF strategy to ensure our TypeScript types remained reliable across updates.

Q: What kind of projects did you handle at DigitalChefs?
A: I built native apps using React Native for small and medium clients. One of the more complex ones was for the KLM flight crew to manage business class orders. I also built a component library with custom navigation to standardize our projects, and an ExpressJS system to handle the app data.

Q: What technology did you use for the pipeline inspection tools?
A: That was at IT-Transit. We used Flex and ActionScript primarily, along with JavaScript. The software tools were for landscape measurements and pipe inspections within an engineering CMS platform. I also implemented a REST API to connect client services for generating renovation progress statistics.

Q: What is your experience with embedded systems?
A: At ABiggerCircle, I developed entertainment system modules using BackboneJS, jQuery, and Gulp. These were for devices in closed network environments, like ships in the ocean. I had to implement complex audio control logic to manage captain notifications, ensuring they overrode the entertainment audio.

Q: Why did you use a local LLM for testing at Mobiquity instead of the live API?
A: It was primarily a budget decision. Running extensive integration tests via Playwright against a live paid API burns through tokens very quickly. By spinning up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock, we saved significant budget while still validating that our agentic chat UI handled responses correctly.

Q: How did you ensure type safety between Frontend and Backend at Mobiquity?
A: I worked with the Backend team to implement a BFF (Backend for Frontend) strategy. The key was steering the BE work to generate reliable TypeScript types that we could consume directly in the frontend. This minimized runtime errors and kept our contracts in sync.

Q: What was the most challenging legacy system you had to deal with?
A: Definitely the WebSphere monolith at EriksDigital. We had to migrate it to a hybrid micro-frontend setup. The code was old and undocumented, so I had to reverse-engineer modules to understand the logic before we could rewrite them. It was a massive effort to improve performance without breaking existing functionality.

Q: Did you ever work on apps for airline crews?
A: Yes, at DigitalChefs. I built a React Native app specifically for KLM business class crews. It managed passenger requests, including food and drink orders. It was a complex system because it had to be reliable for the crew while interacting with an ExpressJS backend for data management.

Q: What were the challenges with the embedded work at ABiggerCircle?
A: The main challenge was the environment—these systems were running on ships in the ocean, in a closed network. I used BackboneJS and jQuery to build entertainment modules, but I also had to implement logic for audio controls so that captain notifications would properly interrupt the entertainment system. It required very precise state management.

Q: What's your current hardware setup for development?
A: I use a MacBook Pro 16 M2 and a Mac Mini M2. I have a bit of a unique monitor setup: an ultra-wide as my main screen, and an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen in portrait mode specifically for mobile UI development. I also switch mice depending on the task—Razer for design work, Magic Mouse for coding.

Q: When do you prefer Vanilla JS over a framework?
A: If I'm building a lightweight web page where SEO and complex state management aren't the primary concerns, I prefer Vanilla JS paired with SCSS and Vite. It keeps the bundle size minimal and the performance high. But for high-traffic, SEO-critical applications, I always go with NextJS.

Q: What did you learn from your time at Luxoft?
A: That was early in my career in Ukraine. I worked on Automotive UI for car entertainment systems. I learned a lot about strict code review processes and Git repository management while supporting senior developers. It set a strong foundation for how I handle version control and code quality now.

Q: How did you manage the legacy modules at EriksDigital?
A: It was a complex migration from a WebSphere monolith. Many modules were old and lacked documentation. I had to reverse-engineer the logic to understand the dependencies before we could decouple them into a micro-frontend architecture. It was risky, but necessary to unblock the team and improve our deployment velocity.

Q: What was the specific tech stack for the DigitalChefs airline app?
A: We used React Native for the mobile app itself. For the backend, I built a system using ExpressJS to manage the data and statistics—basically a custom CMS for the flight crew's orders. I also built a custom component library to handle the specific navigation requirements of the crew's workflow.

Q: What's your strategy for writing reliable end-to-end tests?
A: I rely on Playwright. It's fast and reliable. At Mobiquity, I used it for our Chat UI. The key was mocking the backend services properly. We used a local LLM to mock the Python BE responses, which made our tests deterministic and free to run, rather than flaky and expensive like they would be against a live AI API.

Q: How did you handle the SEO requirements at A-Dam?
A: That was the main driver for migrating to NextJS. The original React app wasn't cutting it for search engines. By moving to NextJS with Server-Side Rendering (SSR), we ensured that the crawlers saw the full content immediately. The page load speed improved 5x, which also gave us a massive SEO boost.

Q: What did you use for the notification system at Mobiquity?

I worked very closely with the backend team to ensure the API specs were tight, using a BFF pattern to keep our types synchronized.

Q: What's your preferred OS for development?
A: MacOS, hands down. I run a MacBook Pro 16 M2 and a Mac Mini M2. The Unix base makes everything easier for web dev. I pair it with a Magic Mouse for development work, though I switch to a Razer mouse if I'm doing design stuff.

Q: Have you worked with WebSockets?
A: Yes, heavily at Mobiquity. We used WebSockets for the live chat functionality in the Agentic Chat UI. It was integrated with a Python backend. The challenge was ensuring the connection was stable and handling the real-time stream of data from the agent without UI stutter.

Q: How do you handle middleware in NextJS?
A: I use it for routing logic and blocking. For the dating platform project at Mobiquity, I actually used Axios Interceptors as a form of middleware to steer user stories. If a user didn't meet certain browser properties or onboarding criteria, I'd block the route and redirect them. It keeps the component logic clean.

Q: What was the hardest part of the Chat UI build at Mobiquity?
A: The integration between the Python backend and the React frontend was tricky because of the dual communication channels. We used RestAPI for the initial agent configuration and context setting, but switched to WebSockets for the actual live chat stream. Keeping the state synchronized between those two protocols required very clean handling in the React hooks.

Q: Did you utilize any specific testing frameworks for the Mobiquity chat agent?
A: Yes, I used Playwright for integration tests. The cool part was that we didn't want to pay for API tokens during testing, so I set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock server. It allowed us to run full end-to-end flows in our pipeline without hitting the budget.

Q: How did you manage the data for the KLM crew app?
A: I built a custom CMS using ExpressJS to handle the app data and statistics. The React Native app needed to sync passenger requests (food/drinks) reliably, so the backend had to be lightweight but robust. I also built a component library to ensure the UI remained consistent across different screens for the crew.

Q: What's your opinion on Tailwind CSS?
A: I use it in my core stack now. It's great for consistency. At Mobiquity, we used it heavily. However, if I'm doing a lightweight vanilla JS project with Vite, I might stick to SCSS. But for a large React/NextJS app, Tailwind speeds up development significantly.

A: I prefer Webstorm, always in dark mode (I usually work in a dark room). I've also started using Cursor and Claude Code to speed things up. I'm picky about formatting—always spaces, never tabs. Consistency is everything.

Q: What did you work on for the maritime embedded systems?
A: At ABiggerCircle, I worked on entertainment modules for ships. The stack was BackboneJS, jQuery, and Gulp. The hard part was the logic to manage system notifications—like if the captain needed to speak, the audio controls had to override the movie or music immediately. It was a closed network environment, so debugging was... interesting.

A: You can't rely on live AI APIs for CI/CD—it's too expensive and non-deterministic. At Hexaware, I set up a local LLM (GPT OSS 2.0) to act as a mock. This ensured our Playwright tests were hitting a consistent endpoint with predictable latency and responses, saving our budget and our sanity.

Q: What's the most 'hacky' part of your hardware setup?
A: Probably my monitor setup. I use a standard ultra-wide, but I have an Asus 14-inch Zenscreen turned vertically (portrait mode) right next to it. It's dedicated solely to mobile UI review. It looks a bit odd, but it's the best way to develop mobile-first web apps on a desktop.

Q: How did you optimize the Monolith at EriksDigital?

Q: What backend tech have you touched recently?
A: At Mobiquity, the backend was Python (for the LLM agent), but I've also worked with NestJS and ExpressJS in the past. At DigitalChefs, I built a custom CMS with ExpressJS. I'm comfortable defining API specs and working on the BFF layer to ensure the frontend gets clean data.

Q: What tools do you use for personal projects?
A: Right now, I'm using Github Actions for CI/CD. I'm building my portfolio website. I also use Claude Code and Cursor to accelerate development. I'm really interested in local LLMs, so I'm experimenting with running private agents on my Mac Mini M2.

Q: Did you ever work with automotive systems?

The constraints are different than web—you have to worry about strict memory limits and, in the case of the ships, overriding audio for safety announcements.

Q: What was the benefit of using LangChain in your chat project?
A: In the Agentic Chat UI at Mobiquity, LangChain allowed us to abstract the interaction with the LLM. It made it easier to chain the context from the initial RestAPI configuration into the WebSocket-based live chat. It provided a structured way to handle the agent's 'memory' and context window, which was crucial for the banking demo we were building.

Q: How do you handle state management in complex apps?
A: It depends on the scope. For something like the notification system at Mobiquity, I used React Context for local state and leveraged the cache from our API calls (via tools like TanStack Query). For the embedded entertainment systems I worked on earlier, we had to be much more manual with BackboneJS models to sync the state between the audio controls and the UI.

Q: What was the hardest bug you tracked down in the embedded project?
A: In the maritime system at ABiggerCircle, we had an issue where the captain's announcement wouldn't reliably mute the movie audio. It turned out to be a race condition in the event handling between the Jquery UI and the backbone model that interfaced with the hardware. Debugging that on a closed network without standard remote tools was... character building.

Q: How do you ensure your CSS scales?
A: I'm a big proponent of Tailwind CSS now. It enforces consistency and prevents the 'stylesheet sprawl' you get with traditional CSS. At Mobiquity, it helped our team move fast without fighting over class names. If I have to use SCSS, I'm very strict about modularity, but Tailwind is just more efficient for large teams.

Q: What's your take on Micro-Frontends?
A: They are a necessary evil for large scale. At EriksDigital, we moved from a monolith to micro-frontends not because it was trendy, but because we needed to decouple the teams and deployment cycles. It adds complexity—orchestration, shared state, consistent styling—but for a massive legacy system like that WebSphere app, it was the only way to modernize incrementally.

Q: How do you configure your CI/CD pipelines?
A: I've used Azure Pipelines extensively, specifically at Mobiquity for the CMS project. I like to keep the pipeline definitions close to the code. For my personal projects, I'm using Github Actions. The key is automating the testing—like that Playwright + Local LLM setup—so you catch issues before merge.

I'm comfortable diving into whatever the stack requires—'Superstar Factor' and all that—but my deep expertise is in the Frontend/BFF layer.

A: I see them as the logical evolution of the SSR work I did at A-Dam. Reducing the bundle size sent to the client is critical for mobile performance. While the paradigm shift is tricky, being able to fetch data directly in the component on the server side simplifies the architecture significantly compared to the old `getServerSideProps` pattern.

Q: How did you handle communication between micro-frontends at EriksDigital?

Shared state was kept to a minimum—mostly just user session data—to prevent the 'distributed monolith' problem.

Q: What's your strategy for handling large forms in React?
A: I avoid managing form state manually if I can help it. I prefer libraries like React Hook Form because they minimize re-renders by not binding every keystroke to the main component state. Q: How do you handle feature flags?

Q: What makes Playwright better than Cypress for you?
A: Parallelization and speed. Playwright runs faster and handles multiple tabs/windows much better than Cypress. For the Chat UI testing, the ability to easily mock network requests at the browser layer was a huge win for stabilizing our CI pipeline.

Q: How do you document your code?
A: I prefer self-documenting code with strong typing (TypeScript) and clear naming. For complex logic, I write decision records (ADRs) rather than just inline comments. At EriksDigital, documentation was missing for the legacy system, so as we migrated, I made sure we documented the *why* of the architecture, not just the *how*.

Q: What was the specific technical win with the local LLM mock?

This allowed our Playwright tests to assert that the UI correctly rendered charts or tables based on specific token streams, without flaking due to network lag.

Q: How do you handle routing in your current projects?

Q: What's the most annoying thing about embedded JS?

Q: How do you maintain CSS at scale?
A: Tailwind CSS is my default. It enforces a design system without the overhead of maintaining a massive SCSS architecture. At Mobiquity, it allowed our team to move fast without breaking styles across the CMS. Consistency is the hardest part of CSS, and Tailwind solves that.

Q: How did you optimize the A-Dam site so much?
